title: The physician
hook: court physician in Cairo, he advised moderation in everything

segments.voice: Yesterday, De'ot, the laws of character, and your line: the body serves the soul. At which meal did you stop with a little room left? Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

A courtyard full of people, waiting. Some are Jews, some are not. Some are officials, some are ordinary people. They're all waiting for one tired man to ride home. That's the scene Maimonides himself describes in a letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon, the man translating his work. He writes that he goes up to Cairo early in the day to attend the ruler's household, and comes back to find his house surrounded by patients. He barely eats before he starts seeing them, and he keeps going into the night. Today's word is what he did for a living.
screen: `A COURTYARD FULL OF PATIENTS.` → `A LETTER TO HIS TRANSLATOR.` → `CAIRO BY DAY, PATIENTS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The physician. In Hebrew, rofe. Turn it four ways. First, the job. The man who wrote a code of all Jewish law and a philosophical guide also earned his living by medicine, serving at the court and treating ordinary people at home. The scholar and the doctor were the same person on the same day. Second, the advice. His medical writings keep returning to one idea we've already met in his ethics: moderation. Not too much food, not too little. Exercise, but don't exhaust yourself. Sleep in its season. And he pays attention to the mind as well as the body: worry, grief and anger, he warns, take a toll on health, and a settled, cheerful spirit helps a person heal. Third, the link. His law code gives advice a doctor might give, about meals and sleep. His medical advice turns to the temper of the mind. The same measure, not too much and not too little, runs through both. For him, medicine and ethics are one way of thinking, applied twice. Fourth, the healer behind the healer. The Torah has God say, "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." A doctor who believes that doesn't stop practicing medicine. Maimonides worked, prescribed and wrote. For him, caring for the body and trusting God were not rivals. The tired man in the courtyard is doing both at once, patient by patient, until the lamps are lit.
screen: `SCHOLAR AND DOCTOR, SAME DAY.` · `MODERATION IN EVERYTHING.` · `ONE MEASURE FOR BODY AND MIND.` · `I AM THE LORD THAT HEALETH THEE.` · then, large: `MODERATION.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to take a walk. If you can, stand up now and walk slowly, around the room or down a hallway, for the length of the bell. Not fast, not for a step count. A middle pace. Feel your heels land and your weight shift. Let your breath match your steps. If you can't walk right now, sit, and walk in your mind: picture a short route you know, step by step, at an easy pace. Either way, aim for not too much and not too little. The bell holds the time.
The physician. Rofe in Hebrew: Maimonides earned his living as a doctor, and his medicine and his ethics give the same advice. Moderation. Today's word.
Your line: moderation. Today, catch one thing you tend to overdo, coffee, screens, work, and take it down just one notch. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition honors medicine as a calling, and Jewish law expects a sick person to seek a doctor's care; some Jews read Maimonides' medical advice alongside his laws of character.

fork.setup: you're Maimonides. you've spent the day at court in Cairo. you ride home, exhausted, and find your courtyard full of people waiting. what do you do?
options: send them all home until tomorrow.
eat a little, then see patients into the night.
fork.reveal: in his letter, he describes eating briefly and then treating patients, Jews and non-Jews, high and low, into the night.

original.note: Hebrew: a physician or healer, from the same root as the verb in "the LORD that healeth thee."

trapdoor: what you thought: Maimonides was a rabbi who wrote books.
what it means: he was also a working physician, and his medical advice matches his ethics: moderation.
what a scholar hears: the letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon, the medical regimens, and the doctrine of the mean applied to body and soul alike.

notes: The hook and fork paraphrase Maimonides' letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon (going to Cairo early to attend the court, returning to find the courtyard full of patients, Jews and non-Jews, eating briefly, seeing patients into the night). Please confirm the details; no date given.
'Serving at the court' kept general (the letter speaks of the ruler/sultan's household); please confirm.
Emotions affecting health is from his medical regimens (Regimen of Health); paraphrased and general. Please confirm.
Healing the sick soul like a sick body: Eight Chapters ch. 3 and De'ot 2:1; please confirm.
